transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-22
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CTO - Aquifer), Samir Patel (Platform Lead), Hannah Lee (ML Eng), Jon Ortiz (SRE)

Summary: quick discovery on p95 / concurrency / streaming readiness. Customer wants a plan to ensure sub-500ms p95 for short completions, and graceful fallback to cheaper model when burst saturates. They want both Hosted and Dedicated tradeoffs explored and an initial token/sec benchmark run.

Topics: p95 targets, token/sec benchmarking, streaming vs batch, KV/prefix cache, autoscale bumping, private VPC constraints, SOC2/KMS, canary failover policies

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE — Diego our SE is here. Can you quick round robin intro?
[00:12] Priya: Priya, CTO at Aquifer Analytics. We're rebuilding an insights pipeline that uses streaming summarization and interactive QnA. Need to be realtime-ish, p95 targets around 400–600ms for short answers.
[00:25] Samir: Samir, platform. Responsible for infra and cost. We care about predictable tail latency and also cost per token.
[00:35] Diego: thanks. Quick note, when you say 400 to 600ms p95, is that end-to-end or purely inference?
[00:42] Priya: good Q. That's user-perceived end to end — so includes network and some postprocessing. Inference target we'd like ~250–350ms p95 for common 16–64 token responses.
[00:54] Hannah: and we stream tokens back to the UI, so chunked response latency matters, not just final token.
[01:05] Jon: SRE here, concerned about burst behavior — if a campaign launches we'll see a spike of concurrent sessions. Want graceful degradation, not hard errors.
[01:15] Maya: perfect. So main goals: p95 sub-350ms inference for short spans, streaming behavior that doesn't increase tail too much, and fallback to cheaper model at scale. We'll cover Hosted, Dedicated, and Private tradeoffs.
[01:28] Diego: quick note on benchmarking approach — we usually run token/sec baseline with both steady-state and burst tests. We instrument KV cache hit-rate sim to show prefix caching benefits.
[01:40] Samir: what about quantized variants? We want to save cost but not degrade quality for our prompts.
[01:46] Diego: yes, quantization options can drop memory and cost. We'll suggest a profile: float16 for latency-critical, int8/4 for cost-optimized Dedicated. But need evals.
[01:58] Priya: what about private deployment? We have regs that require VPC egress control, so private control plane might be needed.
[02:06] Maya: we have Private (VPC) with customer-managed networking and KMS integration. There is an extra onboarding timeline and license fee, but it enables no-data-leak and HSM/KMS integration.
[02:18] Jon: how intrusive is the private control plane? we cannot route traffic through a public internet egress.
[02:24] Diego: we do a direct peering or VPN setup. The inference nodes sit in your VPC in the Private offering. For Hosted, we support VPC endpoints for limited flows but it's not full on-prem.
[02:36] Hannah: on the streaming semantics — do you support chunked streaming with partial tokens and reconnect? we need to resume a stream if connection drops.
[02:44] Diego: we support streaming with incremental flushes and connection-aware resume, but the resume path is best-effort. We rely on KV cache and prefix checkpoints to avoid regen from scratch.
[02:56] Priya: risks: if we have 10k concurrent streams, how do you keep p95?
[03:03] Diego: two levers: autoscale pools + burst queues and routing policy. Dedicated allows reserved GPU pools sized to hold high concurrency; Hosted can route to cheaper cohorts or fallback to smaller models under overload.
[03:15] Samir: can you do model variants automatically — like if the main large model is saturated switch to a distilled variant?
[03:21] Maya: yes, smart routing and automatic fallback can route by policy. Canary, A/B or cost-based fallback. Diego will show a sketch later.
[03:31] [05:00] Diego: (shares screen) here's an example arch: requests enter API, policy layer routes by latency SLO, cost, region, and then the runtime chooses kernel and batching strategy. We also have prefix cache to avoid re-tokenizing repeated prompts.
[05:20] Samir: how big is the KV cache overhead? memory wise?
[05:25] Diego: depends on sequence lengths and hit rate. For typical prompt shapes, it's a modest % of model memory; you can configure TTLs and shard it per model.
[05:35] [07:10] Hannah: we do a lot of short 20–40 token answers then a few 300 token summaries. Would batching help us or hurt latency?
[07:19] Diego: continuous batching helps throughput at cost of some latency — we can set adaptive batching thresholds so short requests bypass batching to keep p95 low, while longer ones batch for throughput.
[07:30] Priya: show of hands — are you suggesting different execution profiles per route?
[07:34] Diego: exactly: per-route profiles. For UI chat route we do low latency profile, for background summarization we do high throughput profile with quantization.
[07:45] [10:02] Jon: question about metrics and tracing. We need token-level cost breakdown and per-request traces for audits.
[10:10] Maya: Redwood Console exposes token-level gating, model-level cost, per-route latency breakdown, and tracing hooks you can forward to your tracing stack.
[10:22] Samir: we need audit logs and SSO with SCIM and SAML.
[10:27] Maya: supported. We'll include a security pack with SSO, RBAC, SOC2 artifacts, and KMS/HSM integration details.
[10:36] [12:00] Priya: let's get specific on benchmarks. We want p95 < 350ms for 16–64 token responses, and sustain 5,000 tokens/sec during normal day, with burst to 50k tokens/sec for 10 minutes during marketing pushes. Is that plausible?
[12:17] Diego: numbers look plausible but will depend on model choice and batch shapes. For a 13B-ish open model on Dedicated GPUs you can reach high token/sec with batching; streaming p95 at 350ms is harder at very high concurrency. We'll propose a hybrid: Dedicated pool sized for baseline and Hosted bursts + fallback to smaller model.
[12:36] Hannah: can we get deterministic p95 guarantees from Dedicated?
[12:41] Maya: Dedicated with reserved capacity gives much more predictable p95, and we can set SLOs in contract.
[12:48] Samir: curious about cost math — send a sample projection for 5k steady and 50k burst using mixed routing.
[12:56] Maya: yes, action item to provide sample run-rate and burst pricing.
[13:03] [15:40] Diego: architecture note — for streaming with resume we keep KV cache checkpoint and a small prefix snapshot to allow a resumed request to continue without regen. This reduces tail on reconnects.
[15:50] Priya: if a model falls back how do you keep response quality consistent? we can't have wildly different answers between big model and distilled.
[15:59] Diego: we'll recommend a staged evaluation and a fallback policy that maps to compatible model family so outputs are similar; we also support reranking and QA checks to maintain quality.
[16:10] Samir: do you have any prebuilt rerankers or comparator scores to detect regressions on fallback?
[16:16] Diego: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts that can be tied to prompt sets. We can run holdout prompts and alert when similarity drops.
[16:28] [18:00] Hannah: for the token/sec test, what harness do you need from us?
[18:05] Diego: a representative prompt set, session concurrency shape, and a few traces showing token lengths. Ideally TB of examples but 1000 varied examples is a good start.
[18:16] Samir: we'll dump 1,000 traces by tomorrow.
[18:21] Priya: timeline — we want a pilot next month. How long to stand up Dedicated pilot?
[18:28] Maya: typically Dedicated pilot with reserved pool takes 2–4 weeks depending on size and procurement. Private/VPC adds onboarding steps. Hosted PO C can start within days.
[18:37] [20:00] Jon: procurement question: do you support SOC2 compliance reports and do you allow an on-prem option?
[20:07] Maya: yes to SOC2. On-prem is available as a Private package for regulated use-cases but it is a separate process.
[20:16] Samir: for the burst of 50k tokens/sec, do you recommend vertical scale (bigger GPUs) or horizontal (more smaller GPUs)?
[20:23] Diego: depends on model optimizer and sequence lengths. Horizontal scaling with many pods and continuous batching often gives better availability and easier autoscale, but larger GPUs can reduce cross-pod KV coordination overhead. We'll propose a mixed pool.
[20:37] [22:00] Hannah: we also need observability: token-level per-route cost and real-time p95 heatmaps for our oncall.
[22:08] Maya: Redwood Console shows per-route dashboards, and we can forward traces to Datadog/Lightstep.
[22:18] Priya: can we throttle specific orgs or users during a burst?
[22:22] Diego: yes, rate-limits and per-token quotas per token bucket are supported; you can also set priority-based routing.
[22:30] [24:40] Samir: competitors — we've talked to Anthropic and vendor X, they push hosted ease but pricing is less flexible. Why Redwood vs them?
[24:48] Maya: Redwood differentiates on production controls: unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, smart routing, and cost-aware levers. We give more ops-level controls for predictable SLOs.
[24:58] Priya: ok practical next step: run a token/sec baseline and a burst test with our traces and compare Hosted vs Dedicated for p95 and cost.
[25:08] Diego: we'll set up a test plan: steady-state 24h run at 5k tokens/sec, 10x spike windows to simulate marketing bursts, and monitor p95, error rate, and cost per token.
[25:24] Samir: one more — do you support model quantization in hosted? we prefer Dedicated for quantized variants.
[25:30] Diego: hosted has some quantized variants, but Dedicated gives you more control and custom kernel selection.
[25:38] [28:00] Priya: about rollback — if the new model rollout increases regressions, can we do automatic rollback?
[28:07] Diego: yes, rollouts support canary, A/B, and automatic fallback policies; you can tie rollback triggers to accuracy/regression alerts.
[28:18] Hannah: what's the expected network egress when doing 50k tokens/sec? we need to budget bandwidth.
[28:24] Diego: depends on payload and compression; we'll include rough egress estimates in the pricing pack.
[28:36] [30:00] Maya: ok let's align on owners and timeline. Diego will prepare the harness. Maya will send pricing and security pack. Aquifer provides traces and prompt sets. We'll target a bench review in one week.
[30:15] Priya: sounds good. Anything else on concurrency shapes? we have conversational sessions where each session yields many small requests — that pattern increases per-session cost.
[30:25] Diego: we recommend session affinity and KV prefix caching to amortize repeated tokens and reduce per-token compute.
[30:35] Samir: do you have a recommended session cache TTL?
[30:39] Diego: depends on traffic; 10–60s is common for chat sessions, but you can tune per-route.
[30:46] [35:00] Jon: security follow-up — we want to see KMS integration guide and audit log schema.
[35:08] Maya: will include in security pack.
[35:12] Priya: also please include expected latency SLOs per deployment type in the docs.
[35:18] Maya: yes.
[35:22] [40:00] Diego: small demo note — in our internal tests we saw sub-250ms  p95 for 16-token responses on Dedicated optimized kernels w/ small batch bypass. On Hosted at high conc, p95 jumps to ~420ms unless you route to reserved cohorts.
[40:18] Priya: that's in line with our concerns.
[40:24] Samir: okay let's make sure benchmarking tests include cold start scenarios.
[40:29] Diego: will add cold start windows to the test plan.
[40:33] [45:20] Hannah: for the QA alerts, can you tie alerts to Slack channels and create PagerDuty incidents on regression?
[45:28] Diego: yes, Redwood has integrations for Slack and PD. We'll include runbooks.
[45:34] Priya: final ask: can you show an example policy mapping for fallback — large->distilled->cached answer?
[45:41] Diego: yes I'll attach a policy example with the test results.
[45:48] Maya: recap: 1) Aquifer provides traces and prompt set by EOD 23rd; 2) Redwood runs baseline + burst tests and delivers a results sheet; 3) security pack and Dedicated pricing sent by the 25th; 4) bench review meeting scheduled next Tuesday at 14:00 UTC.
[46:10] Priya: agreed.
[46:14] Samir: agreed.
[46:18] Jon: thanks all.
[46:21] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up with invites and the security pack link.
[46:26] [57:30] (call ends, brief off-mic chatter)
